Moonshine shrew neonates emerge at a remarkably modest body mass, with recorded values suggesting a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.933 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.933 grams], a figure derived from comparative data on Crocidura leucodon. This diminutive size is typical of altricial insectivores and places considerable energetic demands on the gestating female. Following parturition, the newborn offspring enter a period of rapid physiological development. The process of weaning, marking the transition from milk dependency to solid food consumption, occurs relatively early in this species. The time since birth at weaning has been estimated at 22 days [tx = estimated at 22 days] based on patterns observed in a related crocidurine species at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This abbreviated suckling stage is an adaptive strategy that allows the female to reduce her own metabolic load and potentially initiate a subsequent litter, reflecting the high reproductive tempo characteristic of small-bodied shrews inhabiting unpredictable environments.

Reproductive output in the Moonshine shrew is constrained by its small body size and high metabolic demands. Field studies indicate that females produce just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], with each litter typically containing two offspring [N_R_i = each litter typically containing two offspring]. This low annual fecundity is offset by a relatively rapid developmental trajectory. Importantly, these reproductive parameters have been documented under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], which approximates the thermal neutral zone for the genus. The gestation period itself, lasting 30 days [tg = 30 days] under these same thermal conditions, is relatively abbreviated for the family, allowing the timing of birth to be synchronized with peaks in invertebrate prey availability in the montane forests of central Africa at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C].

Female Moonshine shrews attain a maximum adult body mass of about 11.8 grams [Wwi = about 11.8 grams], a value that represents the ultimate wet weight for females in this species. This modest size correlates tightly with their elevated basal metabolic demands. Respirometry trials conducted at a thermoneutral temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] have recorded a peak basal metabolic rate of 24.80 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 24.80 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that ranks among the highest mass-specific metabolic rates documented for any terrestrial mammal of comparable size. This energetic intensity necessitates almost continuous foraging and imposes strict physiological constraints on the duration of fasting or torpor that can be tolerated without depleting critical lipid reserves.

The onset of reproductive capability in the Moonshine shrew is preceded by a period of somatic growth and gonadal maturation. Estimates based on life history data from Crocidura leucodon suggest that the time since birth at puberty is roughly 95 days [tp = roughly 95 days], a milestone that typically occurs under ambient thermal conditions near 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Once this threshold is crossed, the reproductively active adult enters a phase of high metabolic demand. The rapid pace of development from neonatal emergence to sexual maturation—occurring in just over three months—is consistent with the strategy of maximizing reproductive output within a brief lifespan. The extended growth phase that follows weaning is characterized by intense feeding activity, as the growing juvenile builds the somatic reserves necessary for its first winter and subsequent breeding season.

Maximum recorded longevity for the Moonshine shrew is approximately 1,095 days [am = approximately 1,095 days], a lifespan estimate derived from captive studies of the congener Crocidura leucodon and measured under controlled temperature conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This duration, equivalent to roughly three years, represents a relatively compressed lifespan for a mammal of this size, though it is extended compared to some northern-hemisphere shrews that experience higher metabolic costs and shorter active seasons. The extended survival under stable laboratory conditions highlights the species' capacity for physiological persistence when environmental stressors are minimized. In natural habitats, lifespan is considerably shorter due to predation pressure, seasonal food shortages, and the energetic costs of maintaining an exceptionally high basal metabolic rate. The interplay between thermal environment and longevity remains a key area for future research into the life history evolution of Afrotropical soricids.
